claim: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), released during hypercapnic challenge, increases calcium oscillations in the chemosensitive parafacial respiratory group (pFRG/RTN).
source: Previously (Forsberg et al., 2016), we revealed that prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), released during hypercapnic challenge, increases calcium oscillations in the chemosensitive parafacial respiratory group (pFRG/RTN).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Forsberg et al., 2016).

claim: pFRG/RTN astrocytes are the PGE2 source.
source: Here, we demonstrate that pFRG/RTN astrocytes are the PGE2 source.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two distinct astrocyte subtypes were found using transgenic mice expressing GFP and MrgA1 receptors in astrocytes.
source: Two distinct astrocyte subtypes were found using transgenic mice expressing GFP and MrgA1 receptors in astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations using transgenic mice as described in the manuscript.

claim: Most astrocytes appeared dormant during time-lapse calcium imaging.
source: Although most astrocytes appeared dormant during time-lapse calcium imaging, a subgroup displayed persistent, rhythmic oscillating calcium activity.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: A subgroup of astrocytes displayed persistent, rhythmic oscillating calcium activity.
source: Although most astrocytes appeared dormant during time-lapse calcium imaging, a subgroup displayed persistent, rhythmic oscillating calcium activity.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Active astrocytes formed a subnetwork within the respiratory network distinct from the neuronal network.
source: These active astrocytes formed a subnetwork within the respiratory network distinct from the neuronal network.
evidence: This is supported by network analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Activation of exogenous MrgA1Rs expressed in astrocytes tripled astrocytic calcium oscillation frequency in both the preBötzinger complex and pFRG/RTN.
source: Activation of exogenous MrgA1Rs expressed in astrocytes tripled astrocytic calcium oscillation frequency in both the preBötzinger complex and pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from MrgA1R activation experiments.

claim: Neurons in the preBötC were unaffected by astrocyte activation.
source: However, neurons in the preBötC were unaffected, whereas neuronal calcium oscillatory frequency in pFRG/RTN doubled.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of neuronal calcium activity after astrocyte activation.

claim: Neuronal calcium oscillatory frequency in pFRG/RTN doubled after astrocyte activation.
source: However, neurons in the preBötC were unaffected, whereas neuronal calcium oscillatory frequency in pFRG/RTN doubled.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of neuronal calcium activity after astrocyte activation.

claim: Astrocyte activation in pFRG/RTN triggered local PGE2 release.
source: Notably, astrocyte activation in pFRG/RTN triggered local PGE2 release and blunted the hypercapnic response.
evidence: This is supported by PGE2 ELISA measurements after astrocyte activation.

claim: Astrocyte activation in pFRG/RTN blunted the hypercapnic response.
source: Notably, astrocyte activation in pFRG/RTN triggered local PGE2 release and blunted the hypercapnic response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced hypercapnic response after astrocyte activation.

claim: Astrocytes play an active role in respiratory rhythm modulation.
source: Thus, astrocytes play an active role in respiratory rhythm modulation, modifying respiratory-related behavior through PGE2 release in the pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Astrocytes modify respiratory-related behavior through PGE2 release in the pFRG/RTN.
source: Thus, astrocytes play an active role in respiratory rhythm modulation, modifying respiratory-related behavior through PGE2 release in the pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing PGE2 release and its effects on respiratory networks.

claim: Astrocytes are able to sense and interact with neurons in a network-specific manner.
source: Increasing evidence indicate that astrocytes are able to sense and interact with neurons in a network-specific manner (Ben Haim and Rowitch, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Astrocytes are involved in respiratory behavior.
source: It has also become evident that astrocytes are involved in respiratory behavior.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) is a brainstem respiratory center.
source: The preBötzinger Complex (preBötC), a brainstem respiratory center (Grass et al., 2004), contain electrically active astrocytes, that exhibit rhythmic calcium (Ca2+) oscillations associated with the respiratory-related neuronal rhythm (Schnell et al., 2011; Okada et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The preBötC contains electrically active astrocytes that exhibit rhythmic calcium oscillations associated with the respiratory-related neuronal rhythm.
source: The preBötzinger Complex (preBötC), a brainstem respiratory center (Grass et al., 2004), contain electrically active astrocytes, that exhibit rhythmic calcium (Ca2+) oscillations associated with the respiratory-related neuronal rhythm (Schnell et al., 2011; Okada et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Brainstem astrocytes respond to changes in blood gas levels.
source: Further, brainstem astrocytes respond to changes in blood gas levels (Angelova et al., 2015), especially in the chemosensitive region the parafacial respiratory group/retrotrapezoid nucleus (pFRG/RTN) (Huckstepp et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During the hypercapnic response, carbon dioxide (CO2) causes ATP release from astrocytes.
source: During the hypercapnic response, carbon dioxide (CO2) causes ATP release from astrocytes (Fukuda et al., 1978; Erlichman et al., 2010; Gourine et al., 2010; Huckstepp et al., 2010; Turovsky et al., 2015; Turovsky et al., 2016), increasing inspiratory frequency (Lorier et al., 2007; Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ATP release from astrocytes increases inspiratory frequency.
source: During the hypercapnic response, carbon dioxide (CO2) causes ATP release from astrocytes (Fukuda et al., 1978; Erlichman et al., 2010; Gourine et al., 2010; Huckstepp et al., 2010; Turovsky et al., 2015; Turovsky et al., 2016), increasing inspiratory frequency (Lorier et al., 2007; Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CO2 elicits a gap junction-dependent release of PGE2.
source: We recently provided evidence that CO2 also elicits a gap junction-dependent release of PGE2 (Forsberg et al., 2016), increasing the signaling frequency of the pFRG/RTN (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: PGE2 increases the signaling frequency of the pFRG/RTN.
source: We recently provided evidence that CO2 also elicits a gap junction-dependent release of PGE2 (Forsberg et al., 2016), increasing the signaling frequency of the pFRG/RTN (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN express the primary enzyme involved in PGE2 synthesis (mPGEs-1).
source: Astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN express the primary enzyme involved in PGE2 synthesis (i.e., mPGEs-1), and might be responsible for the PGE2 release during hypercapnia (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN might be responsible for the PGE2 release during hypercapnia.
source: Astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN express the primary enzyme involved in PGE2 synthesis (i.e., mPGEs-1), and might be responsible for the PGE2 release during hypercapnia (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on previous findings, indicated by the word 'might'.

claim: GFP was expressed in the pFRG/RTN and preBötC of the GFAPMrgA1+ mice.
source: Expression of GFP in the pFRG/RTN and preBötC of the GFAPMrgA1+ mice was evident (Figure 1), and GFP was co-localized with GFAP immunolabeling (Figure 1b and h, n = 11 slices; see Supplementary file 1 for the number of times each experiment was conducted).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and Figure 1.

claim: GFP was co-localized with GFAP immunolabeling.
source: Expression of GFP in the pFRG/RTN and preBötC of the GFAPMrgA1+ mice was evident (Figure 1), and GFP was co-localized with GFAP immunolabeling (Figure 1b and h, n = 11 slices; see Supplementary file 1 for the number of times each experiment was conducted).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1b and h.

claim: 12 ± 3% of the GFP-positive cells in the respiratory networks expressed the astrocyte and oligodendrocyte marker S100β.
source: The astrocyte and oligodendrocyte marker S100β was expressed by 12 ± 3% of the GFP-positive cells in the respiratory networks (n = 409 S100β and 3527 GFP positive cells, 13 slices).
evidence: This is based on quantitative immunohistochemistry data.

claim: 92 ± 4% of the S100β-positive cells also expressed GFP.
source: Conversely, 92 ± 4% of the S100β-positive cells also expressed GFP (Figure 1c and i, n = 13 slices).
evidence: This is based on quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1c and i.

claim: GFAP antibody penetration in immunohistochemistry experiments only reached 24 ± 8% of the brainstem slice thickness.
source: Notably, GFAP antibody penetration in our immunohistochemistry experiments only reached 24 ± 8% of the brainstem slice thickness (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is based on z-projection analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Limited antibody penetration could explain the low ratio of S100β-GFP double-labeled cells.
source: This could explain the low ratio of S100β-GFP double-labeled cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody penetration data.

claim: When only the portion of the slice where S100β-positive cells were found was included, 44 ± 11% of the GFP-positive cells also expressed S100β.
source: When the data was re-analyzed with only the portion of the slice where S100β-positive cells were found included, 44 ± 11% of the GFP-positive cells also expressed S100β.
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: GFP-positive cells followed the neuronal spread.
source: The GFP-positive cells followed the neuronal spread, but expressed neither the neuronal markers NK1R or MAP2 (Figure 1d,e and j,k, n = 1254 cells, 21 slices), nor the microglial marker Iba1 (Figure 1f and l, n = 248 cells, 11 slices).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: GFP-positive cells did not express the neuronal markers NK1R or MAP2.
source: The GFP-positive cells followed the neuronal spread, but expressed neither the neuronal markers NK1R or MAP2 (Figure 1d,e and j,k, n = 1254 cells, 21 slices), nor the microglial marker Iba1 (Figure 1f and l, n = 248 cells, 11 slices).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1d,e,j,k.

claim: GFP-positive cells did not express the microglial marker Iba1.
source: The GFP-positive cells followed the neuronal spread, but expressed neither the neuronal markers NK1R or MAP2 (Figure 1d,e and j,k, n = 1254 cells, 21 slices), nor the microglial marker Iba1 (Figure 1f and l, n = 248 cells, 11 slices).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1f and l.

claim: No GFP expression was detected in littermate controls (WT).
source: No GFP expression was detected in littermate controls (WT; Figure 1m, n = 12 slices).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1m.

claim: The GFAP-driven expression of GFP (and thus MrgA1R) is astrocyte specific.
source: Although we cannot fully exclude that a minority of GFAP expressing cells could be undifferentiated precursor cells, our findings strongly suggest that the GFAP-driven expression of GFP (and thus MrgA1R) is astrocyte specific, as expected (Brenner et al., 1994; Fiacco et al., 2007; Cao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the immunohistochemistry data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Brainstem slices derived from GFAPMrgA1+ and WT control mice displayed similar Ca2+ signaling activity.
source: The Ca2+ time-lapse imaging of brainstem slices derived from both GFAPMrgA1+ and WT control mice displayed similar Ca2+ signaling activity (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Ca2+ signaling frequency was similar between GFAPMrgA1+ and WT mice in the pFRG/RTN (4.9 ± 0.8 cycles/min vs 4.9 ± 0.8 cycles/min, N.S.).
source: This was observed for both frequency (4.9 ± 0.8 cycles/min vs 4.9 ± 0.8 cycles/min, N.S., in the pFRG/RTN and 5.4 ± 1.1 cycles/min vs 5.3 ± 1.0 cycles/min, N.S., in the preBötC, Figure 2b and d)
evidence: This is based on quantitative calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2b and d.

claim: Ca2+ signaling frequency was similar between GFAPMrgA1+ and WT mice in the preBötC (5.4 ± 1.1 cycles/min vs 5.3 ± 1.0 cycles/min, N.S.).
source: This was observed for both frequency (4.9 ± 0.8 cycles/min vs 4.9 ± 0.8 cycles/min, N.S., in the pFRG/RTN and 5.4 ± 1.1 cycles/min vs 5.3 ± 1.0 cycles/min, N.S., in the preBötC, Figure 2b and d)
evidence: This is based on quantitative calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2b and d.

claim: Coefficient of variation was similar between GFAPMrgA1+ and WT mice in the pFRG/RTN (33 ± 10 vs 32 ± 11, N.S.).
source: coefficient of variation (33 ± 10 vs 32 ± 11, N.S., in the pFRG/RTN and 35 ± 9 vs 35 ± 13, N.S., in the preBötC, Figure 2b and d)
evidence: This is based on quantitative calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2b and d.

claim: Coefficient of variation was similar between GFAPMrgA1+ and WT mice in the preBötC (35 ± 9 vs 35 ± 13, N.S.).
source: coefficient of variation (33 ± 10 vs 32 ± 11, N.S., in the pFRG/RTN and 35 ± 9 vs 35 ± 13, N.S., in the preBötC, Figure 2b and d)
evidence: This is based on quantitative calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2b and d.

claim: The induced expression of GFP and MrgA1R did not affect respiratory network activity or function.
source: Thus, the induced expression of GFP and MrgA1R did not affect respiratory network activity or function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of calcium signaling between GFAPMrgA1+ and WT mice.

claim: The MrgA1 mouse line has astrocyte-specific expression of the inserted genes with no physiological effects in the untreated animal.
source: Together with the immunohistochemical expression analyses, this demonstrates that the MrgA1 mouse line has astrocyte-specific expression of the inserted genes. It is also clear that they have no physiological effects in the untreated animal, making this mouse line useful for investigation of the astrocytes role in respiratory networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry and calcium imaging data.

claim: In the pFRG/RTN, 18 ± 13% of the astrocytes were active.
source: In the pFRG/RTN, 18 ± 13% of the astrocytes were active.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: In the pFRG/RTN, 40 ± 12% of the total number of active cells were astrocytes (GFAP+).
source: Of the total number of active cells, 40 ± 12% were astrocytes (GFAP+) (a).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: In the preBötC, 13 ± 7% of the astrocytes were active.
source: In the preBötC, 13 ± 7% of the astrocytes were active, and only 20 ± 9% of the total number of active cells were astrocytes (b).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: In the preBötC, only 20 ± 9% of the total number of active cells were astrocytes.
source: In the preBötC, 13 ± 7% of the astrocytes were active, and only 20 ± 9% of the total number of active cells were astrocytes (b).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: In both the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC, active astrocytes (GFAP+) and neurons (GFAP-) formed separate networks.
source: In both the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC, active astrocytes (GFAP+) and neurons (GFAP-) formed separate networks (f, g).
evidence: This is based on network analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2f and g.

claim: The astrocytic and neuronal networks interconnected to build a joint astrocyte–neuron (GFAP+/GFAP-) network.
source: However, these networks interconnected to build a joint astrocyte–neuron (GFAP+/GFAP-) network (f, g).
evidence: This is based on network analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2f and g.

claim: All subnetworks had similar network properties.
source: All subnetworks had similar network properties (h, j), except the connectivity of the astrocyte–neuron network in the preBötC, which was slightly and nonsignificantly less than that of the other subnetworks (j).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2h and j.

claim: The connectivity of the astrocyte–neuron network in the preBötC was slightly and nonsignificantly less than that of the other subnetworks.
source: All subnetworks had similar network properties (h, j), except the connectivity of the astrocyte–neuron network in the preBötC, which was slightly and nonsignificantly less than that of the other subnetworks (j).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2j.

claim: The pFRG/RTN consisted of equal parts of the three subnetworks.
source: The pFRG/RTN consisted of equal parts of the three subnetworks (i), whereas the preBötC network was predominantly neuronal (k).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The preBötC network was predominantly neuronal.
source: The pFRG/RTN consisted of equal parts of the three subnetworks (i), whereas the preBötC network was predominantly neuronal (k).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2k.

claim: The majority of the astrocytes appeared inactive (82 ± 9% or 208 ± 74 cells per network in the pFRG/RTN).
source: The present study also found that the majority of the astrocytes appeared inactive (Figure 2c and e; 82 ± 9% or 208 ± 74 cells per network in the pFRG/RTN, n = 19 slices; 87 ± 7% or 216 ± 82 cells per network in the preBötC, n = 22 slices).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2c and e.

claim: The majority of the astrocytes appeared inactive (87 ± 7% or 216 ± 82 cells per network in the preBötC).
source: The present study also found that the majority of the astrocytes appeared inactive (Figure 2c and e; 82 ± 9% or 208 ± 74 cells per network in the pFRG/RTN, n = 19 slices; 87 ± 7% or 216 ± 82 cells per network in the preBötC, n = 22 slices).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2c and e.

claim: In the preBötC, the proportion of active astrocytes was similar to that detected by Schnell and colleagues.
source: In the preBötC, the proportion of active astrocytes was similar to that detected by Schnell and colleagues (Schnell et al., 2011), but lower than that reported by both Grass and colleagues (Grass et al., 2004) and Oku and colleagues (Oku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies supported by citations.

claim: In the preBötC, the proportion of active astrocytes was lower than that reported by Grass and colleagues and Oku and colleagues.
source: In the preBötC, the proportion of active astrocytes was similar to that detected by Schnell and colleagues (Schnell et al., 2011), but lower than that reported by both Grass and colleagues (Grass et al., 2004) and Oku and colleagues (Oku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies supported by citations.

claim: This is the first study to describe active and inactive astrocytes within the pFRG/RTN.
source: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to describe active and inactive astrocytes within the pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: There was no difference in the ratio of astrocytes and neurons between the pFRG/RTN and preBötC (70 ± 13% astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN and 61 ± 11% astrocytes in the preBötC, N.S.).
source: We did not see any difference in the ratio of astrocytes and neurons between the two regions (70 ± 13% astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN and 61 ± 11% astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN, N.S.).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of cell populations.

claim: The ratio of astrocytes in organotypic cultures is slightly higher than in acutely frozen and sectioned brainstems.
source: This ratio is slightly higher than what is observed in acutely frozen and sectionend brainstems, where 55 ± 6% of the pFRG/RTN cells (n = 3) and 53 ± 4% of the preBötC cells (n = 6) were astrocytes.
evidence: This is based on comparison between organotypic cultures and acute tissue sections.

claim: The larger proportion of astrocytes compared to neurons could in part be due to reactive gliosis induced by the organotypic brainstem slice culture preparation.
source: The larger proportion of astrocytes compared to neurons could in part be due to reactive gliosis induced by the organotypic brainstem slice culture preparation (Stoppini et al., 1991; Herlenius et al., 2012; Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In living brainstem slice cultures, 40 ± 12% of the active cells in pFRG/RTN were astrocytes (42 ± 27 astrocytes out of 106 ± 62 active cells per network).
source: However, in the living brainstem slice cultures, 40 ± 12% of the active cells in pFRG/RTN were astrocytes (42 ± 27 astrocytes out of 106 ± 62 active cells per network), whereas only 20 ± 9% of active cells in the preBötC were astrocytes (29 ± 17 out of 146 ± 39 active cells per network; Figure 2c and e, p<0.05 when comparing the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC, n = 41; see Supplementary file 2 for a list of all statistical tests used for all comparisons in the present study).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2c and e.

claim: Only 20 ± 9% of active cells in the preBötC were astrocytes (29 ± 17 out of 146 ± 39 active cells per network).
source: However, in the living brainstem slice cultures, 40 ± 12% of the active cells in pFRG/RTN were astrocytes (42 ± 27 astrocytes out of 106 ± 62 active cells per network), whereas only 20 ± 9% of active cells in the preBötC were astrocytes (29 ± 17 out of 146 ± 39 active cells per network; Figure 2c and e, p<0.05 when comparing the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC, n = 41; see Supplementary file 2 for a list of all statistical tests used for all comparisons in the present study).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2c and e.

claim: The proportion of active astrocytes was significantly different between pFRG/RTN and preBötC (p<0.05).
source: However, in the living brainstem slice cultures, 40 ± 12% of the active cells in pFRG/RTN were astrocytes (42 ± 27 astrocytes out of 106 ± 62 active cells per network), whereas only 20 ± 9% of active cells in the preBötC were astrocytes (29 ± 17 out of 146 ± 39 active cells per network; Figure 2c and e, p<0.05 when comparing the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC, n = 41; see Supplementary file 2 for a list of all statistical tests used for all comparisons in the present study).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the calcium imaging data.

claim: Active astrocytes within the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC formed specific networks that differed from those of non-astrocytes (neurons).
source: On the basis of a correlated cell activity analysis (Smedler et al., 2014; Forsberg et al., 2016), we determined that the active astrocytes within the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC formed specific networks. These networks differed from those of non-astrocytes, that is, neurons (Figure 2f and g; see Supplementary file 1 for the number of times each experiment was conducted), but displayed similar network structures (Figure 2h and j).
evidence: This is based on network analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2f, g, h, and j.

claim: Astrocytic and neuronal networks displayed similar network structures.
source: On the basis of a correlated cell activity analysis (Smedler et al., 2014; Forsberg et al., 2016), we determined that the active astrocytes within the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC formed specific networks. These networks differed from those of non-astrocytes, that is, neurons (Figure 2f and g; see Supplementary file 1 for the number of times each experiment was conducted), but displayed similar network structures (Figure 2h and j).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2h and j.

claim: There was an average of 5.8 ± 1.1 cells per cluster, where each neuron connected to on average 4.9 ± 0.9 other neurons.
source: Defining a cluster as Hartelt and colleagues (Hartelt et al., 2008), we found an average of 5.8 ± 1.1 cells per cluster, where each neuron connected to on average 4.9 ± 0.9 other neurons.
evidence: This is based on network analysis using a definition from previous literature.

claim: The astrocytic network showed 6.2 ± 1.3 cells per cluster and 3.8 ± 1.1 connections to other astrocytes.
source: The astrocytic network showed similar connections between each other (6.2 ± 1.3 cells per cluster and 3.8 ± 1.1 connections to other astrocytes).
evidence: This is based on network analysis of astrocytic calcium activity.

claim: For the pFRG/RTN, there were 4.9 ± 0.8 neurons and 5.6 ± 1.8 astrocytes per cell-specific cluster.
source: For the pFRG/RTN, there were 4.9 ± 0.8 neurons and 5.6 ± 1.8 astrocytes per cell-specific cluster.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of the pFRG/RTN.

claim: The pFRG/RTN neurons were on average connected to 3.7 ± 0.8 other neurons, and the astrocytes to 3.7 ± 0.9 other astrocytes.
source: The pFRG/RTN neurons were on average connected to 3.7 ± 0.8 other neurons, the astrocytes to 3.7 ± 0.9 other astrocytes.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of the pFRG/RTN.

claim: The analysis of functional connections rendered similar results as the morphological analysis by Hartelt and colleagues regarding the neuronal network.
source: Thus, our analysis of functional connections rendered similar results as the morphological analysis by Hartelt and colleagues regarding the neuronal network.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous morphological studies.

claim: The structure of the functional astrocytic network is novel.
source: The structure of the functional astrocytic network presented here, is novel and underlines their importance.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: There was no difference in network structure between the preBötC and pFRG/RTN.
source: There was no difference in network structure between the preBötC and pFRG/RTN, as previously described (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on network analysis and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The astrocytic and neuronal networks connected with each other at multiple nodes to form the respiratory networks of the pFRG/RTN and of the preBötC.
source: The astrocytic and neuronal networks connected with each other at multiple nodes, and together they formed the respiratory networks of the pFRG/RTN and of the preBötC.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Some active astrocytes specifically displayed correlated Ca2+ activity with NK1R-expressing (respiratory) neurons, where approximately every second astrocytic peak was precisely timed with a neuronal peak.
source: Some of the active astrocytes specifically displayed correlated Ca2+ activity with NK1R-expressing (i.e. respiratory) neurons, where approximately every second astrocytic peak was precisely timed with a neuronal peak (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging observations shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The astrocytic activity and respiratory output are synchronized in the experimental system.
source: This suggests that the astrocytic activity and respiratory output are synchronized in our system, similarly to what have been described in previous studies (Schnell et al., 2011; Okada et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The combined astrocyte-neuron network had larger clusters (7.1 ± 1.3 cells per cluster in preBötC and 6.8 ± 1.4 cells per cluster in the pFRG/RTN).
source: The combined, larger network had larger clusters (7.1 ± 1.3 cells per cluster in preBötC and 6.8 ± 1.4 cells per cluster in the pFRG/RTN).
evidence: This is based on network analysis of the combined astrocyte-neuron network.

claim: In the pFRG/RTN, astrocytes constituted 37 ± 13% of the total network (number of correlating cell pairs).
source: In the pFRG/RTN, astrocytes constituted 37 ± 13% of the total network (number of correlating cell pairs), whereas astrocytes only constituted 16% ± 5% of the preBötC network (p<0.05 when comparing the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC; Figure 2f,g,i and k).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2f, g, i, and k.

claim: Astrocytes only constituted 16% ± 5% of the preBötC network.
source: In the pFRG/RTN, astrocytes constituted 37 ± 13% of the total network (number of correlating cell pairs), whereas astrocytes only constituted 16% ± 5% of the preBötC network (p<0.05 when comparing the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC; Figure 2f,g,i and k).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2f, g, i, and k.

claim: The proportion of astrocytes in the network was significantly different between pFRG/RTN and preBötC (p<0.05).
source: In the pFRG/RTN, astrocytes constituted 37 ± 13% of the total network (number of correlating cell pairs), whereas astrocytes only constituted 16% ± 5% of the preBötC network (p<0.05 when comparing the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC; Figure 2f,g,i and k).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of network data.

claim: There was a significantly larger number of connections between astrocytes and neurons in the pFRG/RTN than in the preBötC (33 ± 12% vs. 24% ± 11% of all correlating cell pairs, p<0.05).
source: We also observed a significantly larger number of connections between astrocytes and neurons in the pFRG/RTN than in the preBötC (33 ± 12% vs. 24% ± 11% of all correlating cell pairs, p<0.05; Figure 2f,g,i and k).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 2f, g, i, and k.

claim: Astrocytes are both independently active and part of the respiratory networks.
source: Thus, astrocytes are both independently active and part of the respiratory networks, but appear to have different actions in the two central pattern generators.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the network analysis data.

claim: Astrocytes appear to have different actions in the two central pattern generators (pFRG/RTN and preBötC).
source: Thus, astrocytes are both independently active and part of the respiratory networks, but appear to have different actions in the two central pattern generators.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differences observed between pFRG/RTN and preBötC.

claim: There is a large heterogeneity of both astrocyte function and astrocyte-neuronal interactions.
source: Previous studies demonstrate a large heterogeneity of both astrocyte function and astrocyte-neuronal interactions (Ben Haim and Rowitch, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Under control conditions, astrocytes displayed a low oscillating frequency (1.1 ± 0.5 cycles/min in the preBötC vs. 1.1 ± 0.4 cycles/min in the pFRG/RTN; difference not statistically significant).
source: Under control conditions, astrocytes displayed a low oscillating frequency (1.1 ± 0.5 cycles/min in the preBötC (n = 22 slices) vs. 1.1 ± 0.4 cycles/min in the pFRG/RTN (n = 19 slices); difference not statistically significant), similar to that described previously for active astrocytes (Grass et al., 2004; Schnell et al., 2011; Okada et al., 2012; Oku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The frequency displayed by the astrocytes in each region was lower than that shown by the neurons in the respective regions.
source: The frequency displayed by the astrocytes in each region was lower than that shown by the neurons in the respective regions (preBötC: 5.4 ± 2.4 cycles/min, n = 22 slices, p<0.05 compared with astrocytes; pFRG/RTN: 6.4 ± 3.5 cycles/min, n = 19 slices, p<0.05 compared with astrocytes, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Application of the MrgA1R ligand FLRF increased the Ca2+-signaling frequency of astrocytes in both the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC.
source: Next, we activated the GFAPMrgA1+ astrocytes by applying the MrgA1R ligand FLRF, which increased the Ca2+-signaling frequency of astrocytes in both the pFRG/RTN and the preBötC (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: In the pFRG/RTN, astrocyte activation induced an increase in the signaling frequency of the non-astrocytes.
source: In the pFRG/RTN, astrocyte activation also induced an increase in the signaling frequency of the non-astrocytes (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: In the preBötC, non-astrocytes retained their Ca2+-signaling frequency independent of astrocyte stimulation.
source: This is in contrast to the preBötC, where non-astrocytes retained their Ca2+-signaling frequency independent of astrocyte stimulation (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Inactive astrocytes exhibited a single Ca2+ peak shortly after the application of FLRF, but returned to the inactive state within 10 s.
source: Inactive astrocytes exhibited a single Ca2+ peak shortly after the application of FLRF, but returned to the inactive state within 10 s (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging observations shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The stimulation of astrocytes did not affect the network structures of the astrocytic, neuronal, or complete respiratory networks.
source: The stimulation of astrocytes did not affect the network structures of the astrocytic, neuronal, or complete respiratory networks (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Astrocytes in slices derived from WT mice did not react to the application of FLRF.
source: Astrocytes in slices derived from WT mice did not react to the application of FLRF (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Astrocytes do not directly modify neuronal activity in the preBötC.
source: While these findings suggest that astrocytes do not directly modify neuronal activity in the preBötC, astrocytes may nonetheless be important for the maintenance of the respiratory rhythm generation in this complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Astrocytes may be important for the maintenance of the respiratory rhythm generation in the preBötC.
source: While these findings suggest that astrocytes do not directly modify neuronal activity in the preBötC, astrocytes may nonetheless be important for the maintenance of the respiratory rhythm generation in this complex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: The astrocyte inhibitor methionine sulfoximine depresses breathing in vivo.
source: For instance, the astrocyte inhibitor methionine sulfoximine depresses breathing in vivo (Young et al., 2005), and glial inhibitors (fluorocitrate, fluoroacetate, and methionine sulfoximine) reduce respiratory-related activity in the preBötC in vitro (Erlichman et al., 1998; Huxtable et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Glial inhibitors (fluorocitrate, fluoroacetate, and methionine sulfoximine) reduce respiratory-related activity in the preBötC in vitro.
source: For instance, the astrocyte inhibitor methionine sulfoximine depresses breathing in vivo (Young et al., 2005), and glial inhibitors (fluorocitrate, fluoroacetate, and methionine sulfoximine) reduce respiratory-related activity in the preBötC in vitro (Erlichman et al., 1998; Huxtable et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hypoxia and mechanical stimulation can induce a Ca2+ influx in preBötC astrocytes, causing a release of ATP.
source: Hypoxia and mechanical stimulation can induce a Ca2+ influx in preBötC astrocytes, causing a release of ATP (Angelova et al., 2015; Rajani et al., 2017), which maintains the inspiratory-related rhythm generation in the preBötC during post-hypoxic depression (Gourine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ATP release from astrocytes maintains the inspiratory-related rhythm generation in the preBötC during post-hypoxic depression.
source: Hypoxia and mechanical stimulation can induce a Ca2+ influx in preBötC astrocytes, causing a release of ATP (Angelova et al., 2015; Rajani et al., 2017), which maintains the inspiratory-related rhythm generation in the preBötC during post-hypoxic depression (Gourine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The ion channels involved in ATP release from astrocytes remain to be determined.
source: Although the ATP release is caused by an increase in [Ca2+]i, the involved ion channels remain to be determined (Rajani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about what is not yet known, supported by citation.

claim: The ion channels involved in ATP release could be different from the ones involved in the MrgA1-induced astrocyte stimulation.
source: These could be different from the ones involved in the MrgA1-induced astrocyte stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental design.

claim: The results indicate a low proportion (~20%) of astrocytes participating in the preBötC network.
source: Further, our results indicate a low proportion (~20%) of astrocytes participating in the preBötC network, and stimulation of these might not be sufficient to affect the neuronal rhythm.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis data.

claim: Stimulation of the low proportion of astrocytes in the preBötC might not be sufficient to affect the neuronal rhythm.
source: Further, our results indicate a low proportion (~20%) of astrocytes participating in the preBötC network, and stimulation of these might not be sufficient to affect the neuronal rhythm.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the data.

claim: Astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN modulate ongoing respiratory network activity.
source: Our data suggest that astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN modulate ongoing respiratory network activity, which is in contrast to their function in the preBötC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Astrocytes are known to modulate synaptic transmission between neurons, but the mechanism remains a mystery.
source: Astrocytes are known to modulate synaptic transmission between neurons, but the mechanism remains a mystery (Ben Haim and Rowitch, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Astrocytes may use connexins to propagate Ca2+ waves.
source: They may also use connexins to propagate Ca2+ waves (Parpura et al., 2012), but we recently showed that gap junction inhibition does not affect the network synchronization of the pFRG/RTN (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gap junction inhibition does not affect the network synchronization of the pFRG/RTN.
source: They may also use connexins to propagate Ca2+ waves (Parpura et al., 2012), but we recently showed that gap junction inhibition does not affect the network synchronization of the pFRG/RTN (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Gap junctions are not likely to constitute the main bridge between the cells during normoxic and normocapnic conditions in the pFRG/RTN.
source: Therefore gap junctions are not likely to constitute the main bridge between the cells during normoxic and normocapnic conditions in the pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previous finding about gap junction inhibition.

claim: Gap junctions can be utilized by astrocytes to release the gliotransmitter ATP.
source: However, gap junctions can be utilized by astrocytes to release the gliotransmitter ATP, and purinergic signaling plays an important role for astrocyte-neuron interactions during hypercapnia (Erlichman et al., 2010; Gourine et al., 2010; Huckstepp et al., 2010; Gourine and Kasparov, 2011; Angelova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Purinergic signaling plays an important role for astrocyte-neuron interactions during hypercapnia.
source: However, gap junctions can be utilized by astrocytes to release the gliotransmitter ATP, and purinergic signaling plays an important role for astrocyte-neuron interactions during hypercapnia (Erlichman et al., 2010; Gourine et al., 2010; Huckstepp et al., 2010; Gourine and Kasparov, 2011; Angelova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Astrocytes release PGE2 in response to a hypercapnic challenge.
source: In addition, we recently suggested that astrocytes also release PGE2 in response to a hypercapnic challenge (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: PGE2 release would in part explain the interaction between chemosensitivity and the inflammatory system.
source: This would in part explain the interaction between chemosensitivity and the inflammatory system observed in several studies (Hofstetter et al., 2007; Siljehav et al., 2012; Siljehav et al., 2014; Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In human neonates, rapid elevation of brainstem PGE2 during infectious events is associated with apnea, bradycardia, and desaturation.
source: Moreover, in human neonates, rapid elevation of brainstem PGE2 during infectious events is associated with, and may explain, the initial presenting symptoms of infection, which are apnea, bradycardia, and desaturation (Siljehav et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Rapid elevation of brainstem PGE2 may explain the initial presenting symptoms of infection in human neonates.
source: Moreover, in human neonates, rapid elevation of brainstem PGE2 during infectious events is associated with, and may explain, the initial presenting symptoms of infection, which are apnea, bradycardia, and desaturation (Siljehav et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Astrocyte stimulation would trigger a PGE2 release similar to that triggered by hypercapnic challenge.
source: Because a hypercapnic challenge triggers a gap junction mediated release of PGE2 (Forsberg et al., 2016), we hypothesized that astrocyte stimulation would trigger a similar release.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings.

claim: After FLRF application, the PGE2 levels in the aCSF doubled in the pFRG/RTN.
source: Indeed, we found that after FLRF application, the PGE2 levels in the artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) doubled in the pFRG/RTN (Figure 4a, n = 8 slices, p<0.05).
evidence: This is based on PGE2 ELISA measurements shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The increase in PGE2 levels after FLRF application was transient.
source: The increase was transient, similar to the PGE2 release that occurs during hypercapnia (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on PGE2 ELISA measurements and comparison with previous findings.

claim: FLRF application did not affect the PGE2 levels in the GFAPMrgA1+ preBötC slices.
source: By contrast, FLRF application did neither affect the PGE2 levels in the GFAPMrgA1+ preBötC slices (n = 3 slices), nor in the pFRG/RTN and preBötC regions in the WT slices (n = 2 slices for each region).
evidence: This is based on PGE2 ELISA measurements.

claim: FLRF application did not affect the PGE2 levels in the pFRG/RTN and preBötC regions in the WT slices.
source: By contrast, FLRF application did neither affect the PGE2 levels in the GFAPMrgA1+ preBötC slices (n = 3 slices), nor in the pFRG/RTN and preBötC regions in the WT slices (n = 2 slices for each region).
evidence: This is based on PGE2 ELISA measurements.

claim: The pFRG/RTN contains chemosensitive astrocytes that release PGE2 upon hypercapnic challenge.
source: These results indicate that the pFRG/RTN contains chemosensitive astrocytes that release PGE2 upon hypercapnic challenge.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PGE2 release data.

claim: The physiological effect of the released PGE2 is likely multifactorial.
source: The physiological effect of the released PGE2 is likely multifactorial.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the complexity of PGE2 signaling.

claim: PGE2 is involved in the stimulation of the pFRG/RTN, similar to the effects of ATP.
source: We previously demonstrated that PGE2 is involved in the stimulation of the pFRG/RTN (Forsberg et al., 2016), similar to the effects of ATP (Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ATP counteracts the vasodilatory effect of CO2/H+ during hypercapnia in the ventral brainstem.
source: Although ATP counteracts the vasodilatory effect of CO2/H+ during hypercapnia in the ventral brainstem (Hawkins et al., 2017), understanding the role of PGE2 in the microcircuits controlling brainstem blood flow will require further investigations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Understanding the role of PGE2 in the microcircuits controlling brainstem blood flow will require further investigations.
source: Although ATP counteracts the vasodilatory effect of CO2/H+ during hypercapnia in the ventral brainstem (Hawkins et al., 2017), understanding the role of PGE2 in the microcircuits controlling brainstem blood flow will require further investigations.
evidence: This is a statement about what needs to be investigated in the future.

claim: Pre-activation of astrocytes blunts the hypercapnic response in the pFRG/RTN.
source: We also determined that pre-activation of astrocytes blunts the hypercapnic response in the pFRG/RTN (Figure 4b, n = 8 slices).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Existing PGE2, and likely other gliotransmitters, is released after activation, depleting the stores.
source: This result suggests that existing PGE2, and likely other gliotransmitters, is released after activation, depleting the stores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the blunted hypercapnic response after astrocyte activation.

claim: Extracellular pH is retained during hypercapnia in the experimental system.
source: Extracellular pH is retained during hypercapnia in our system (Forsberg et al., 2016), but CO2 can pass over the cell membrane and decrease the intracellular pH.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: CO2 can pass over the cell membrane and decrease the intracellular pH.
source: Extracellular pH is retained during hypercapnia in our system (Forsberg et al., 2016), but CO2 can pass over the cell membrane and decrease the intracellular pH.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of CO2 physiology.

claim: Decreased intracellular pH drives bicarbonate and sodium ions into the cell, triggering a Ca2+ influx.
source: This decreased pH drives bicarbonate and sodium ions into the cell, triggering a Ca2+ influx (Turovsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: CO2 can directly modify connexin 26 hemichannels to induce an open state.
source: In parallel, CO2 can directly modify connexin 26 hemichannels to induce an open state (Huckstepp et al., 2010; Meigh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism behind the gliotransmitter release during hypercapnic challenge is possibly different from that of the FLRF-induced activation and Ca2+ influx.
source: Thus, it is possible that the mechanism behind the gliotransmitter release during hypercapnic challenge is different from that of the FLRF-induced activation and Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the different mechanisms of activation.

claim: Hypercapnia did not affect the preBötC activity.
source: Hypercapnia did not affect the preBötC activity (Figure 4c, n = 6 slices), consistent with the results of our previous study (Forsberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4c and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The pFRG/RTN contains astrocytes that are able to react to CO2 and release PGE2 (and possibly other gliotransmitters) to modify the behavior of the neuronal population.
source: In summary, these results indicated that the pFRG/RTN contains astrocytes that are able to react to CO2 and release PGE2 (and possibly other gliotransmitters) to modify the behavior of the neuronal population.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: This type of astrocytic responsiveness and modifying effect was not detected in the preBötC.
source: This type of astrocytic responsiveness and modifying effect was not detected in the preBötC.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing differences between pFRG/RTN and preBötC.

claim: A subgroup of astrocytes with oscillatory Ca2+ activity interacted with and was an essential part of the respiratory neural networks.
source: Taken together, our results led us to conclude that a subgroup of astrocytes with oscillatory Ca2+ activity interacted with and was an essential part of the respiratory neural networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: This is the first study that describes how the astrocytes are organized in a specific network separate from, but interacting with, the neuronal network.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study that describes how the astrocytes are organized in a specific network separate from, but interacting with, the neuronal network.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The release of gliotransmitters is the main signaling system between astrocytes and neurons in respiratory networks.
source: Our results, together with the previous study (Forsberg et al., 2016), strongly suggest that the release of gliotransmitters is the main signaling system.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current and previous studies.

claim: Almost half of the cells in the pFRG/RTN network were astrocytes.
source: Specifically, we observed that almost half of the cells in the pFRG/RTN network were astrocytes and that these astrocytes could entrain the neuronal rhythm, suggesting that gliotransmitters from pFRG/RTN astrocytes can modify respiratory activity.
evidence: This is based on network analysis data.

claim: Astrocytes in the pFRG/RTN could entrain the neuronal rhythm.
source: Specifically, we observed that almost half of the cells in the pFRG/RTN network were astrocytes and that these astrocytes could entrain the neuronal rhythm, suggesting that gliotransmitters from pFRG/RTN astrocytes can modify respiratory activity.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing increased neuronal activity after astrocyte activation.

claim: Gliotransmitters from pFRG/RTN astrocytes can modify respiratory activity.
source: Specifically, we observed that almost half of the cells in the pFRG/RTN network were astrocytes and that these astrocytes could entrain the neuronal rhythm, suggesting that gliotransmitters from pFRG/RTN astrocytes can modify respiratory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: A transient release of PGE2 induced by a Ca2+ influx in the astrocytes of the pFRG/RTN substantially reduced the subsequent hypercapnic response.
source: Moreover, a transient release of PGE2 induced by a Ca2+ influx in the astrocytes of the pFRG/RTN substantially reduced the subsequent hypercapnic response, confirming that PGE2 is one of the central gliotransmitters in chemosensitivity and indicating that it is of astrocytic origin.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing blunted hypercapnic response after astrocyte activation.

claim: PGE2 is one of the central gliotransmitters in chemosensitivity.
source: Moreover, a transient release of PGE2 induced by a Ca2+ influx in the astrocytes of the pFRG/RTN substantially reduced the subsequent hypercapnic response, confirming that PGE2 is one of the central gliotransmitters in chemosensitivity and indicating that it is of astrocytic origin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: PGE2 is of astrocytic origin.
source: Moreover, a transient release of PGE2 induced by a Ca2+ influx in the astrocytes of the pFRG/RTN substantially reduced the subsequent hypercapnic response, confirming that PGE2 is one of the central gliotransmitters in chemosensitivity and indicating that it is of astrocytic origin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing PGE2 release after astrocyte activation.

claim: Subgroups of astrocytes participate in the respiratory rhythm of both the preBötC and the pFRG/RTN.
source: Thus, subgroups of astrocytes participate in the respiratory rhythm of both the preBötC and the pFRG/RTN, and modify respiratory network behavior in the pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Astrocytes modify respiratory network behavior in the pFRG/RTN.
source: Thus, subgroups of astrocytes participate in the respiratory rhythm of both the preBötC and the pFRG/RTN, and modify respiratory network behavior in the pFRG/RTN.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Astrocytes constitute an important link between the respiratory and inflammatory systems.
source: Therefore, we suggest that astrocytes constitute an important link between the respiratory and inflammatory systems, and stand out as a potential target for the treatment of central respiratory dysfunction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and previous literature.

claim: Astrocytes stand out as a potential target for the treatment of central respiratory dysfunction.
source: Therefore, we suggest that astrocytes constitute an important link between the respiratory and inflammatory systems, and stand out as a potential target for the treatment of central respiratory dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The MrgA1R is an endogenous Gq-coupled receptor that is normally not expressed in the brain.
source: The MrgA1R is an endogenous Gq-coupled receptor that is normally not expressed in the brain. Rather, MrgA1R is expressed exclusively in the dorsal root ganglion nociceptive sensory terminals of the spinal cord (Fiacco et al., 2007) and is activated by RF peptides (Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MrgA1R is expressed exclusively in the dorsal root ganglion nociceptive sensory terminals of the spinal cord.
source: The MrgA1R is an endogenous Gq-coupled receptor that is normally not expressed in the brain. Rather, MrgA1R is expressed exclusively in the dorsal root ganglion nociceptive sensory terminals of the spinal cord (Fiacco et al., 2007) and is activated by RF peptides (Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MrgA1R is activated by RF peptides.
source: The MrgA1R is an endogenous Gq-coupled receptor that is normally not expressed in the brain. Rather, MrgA1R is expressed exclusively in the dorsal root ganglion nociceptive sensory terminals of the spinal cord (Fiacco et al., 2007) and is activated by RF peptides (Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Brainstem astrocytes could be selectively activated using synthetic Phe-Leu-Arg-Phe-amide (FLRF).
source: Consequently, we could selectively activate brainstem astrocytes using synthetic Phe-Leu-Arg-Phe-amide (FLRF) (Young et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the experimental design and supported by citations to previous studies.
